questions.stem: A student records the heights of 30 classmates to the nearest cm. What type of data is this?
questions.explanation: Height is continuous data because it can take any value within a range (it is measured, not counted). Even though it's recorded to the nearest cm, the underlying data is continuous. Discrete data can only take specific values (usually whole numbers from counting).

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of discrete data?

options.text: Mass of apples in a bag
Number of pets owned by each student

questions.explanation: Number of pets is discrete because you can only have whole number values (0, 1, 2, 3...). Temperature, mass and time are all continuous as they can take any value within a range.

questions.stem: A researcher collects the following data about cars: colour, engine size (litres), number of doors, fuel type. How many of these are qualitative?
questions.explanation: Colour and fuel type are qualitative (non-numerical, descriptive categories). Engine size is continuous quantitative and number of doors is discrete quantitative. So 2 are qualitative.

questions.stem: Which data collection method would introduce the most bias when investigating favourite school subjects?

options.text: Anonymous online survey sent to all students
Asking every 5th student on the register
Surveying only students in the maths corridor at lunchtime

questions.explanation: Surveying only in the maths corridor introduces location bias: students there are more likely to favour maths. A representative sample should include students from all areas. The other methods provide more random, less biased samples.

questions.stem: Shoe sizes come in values like 5, 5.5, 6, 6.5, 7, etc. What type of data is shoe size?
questions.explanation: Shoe sizes are discrete because they can only take specific fixed values (5, 5.5, 6, etc.). You cannot have a shoe size of 5.3. Even though they include half sizes, the possible values are countable and specific.
